Unless through invasion or under direct and immediate attack, the declaration of war by Congress must then be approved by a vote of the Pacifican public within one week. Failure to get approval by the Pacifican public overturns the declaration of war.

For all acts of war by Pacifica, except in the event of an immediate invasion or attack, the authority of Congress to declare war must be established through a Congressional Declaration of War, as well as a majority cast thereon in a nation-wide referendum. In repelling immediate invasion or attack, the National government may only act within foreign countries for one week without an official Declaration of War, as well as a majority cast thereon in a nation-wide referendum; After six months, and every six months thereafter, both houses of Congress, by affirmative vote and without filibusters, have to approve any extension; If one house votes no on extending, all combat troops must be withdrawn within a year. At times of official peace, the decision to support, aid, assist, or oppose any foreign government or revolutionary movement will be reserved to the People, as Individuals.

Whenever war is declared the Presidency shall immediately conscript and take for use by the government all the public war properties, yards, factories, and supplies, together with employees necessary for their operation.

The Presidency is authorized to use the Pacifican Military as they determine is to be necessary and appropriate in order to defend the State Security of Pacifica. If the presidency and the Military determine they are compelled by a threat posed to Pacifica who under further diplomatic or other peaceful means alone will not adequately protect Pacifica from the continuing threat posed by another nation, the resolution of war powers shall proceed through Congress through specific statutory authorization.

Whenever there is an insurrection in any State against its government, the President may, upon the request of its legislature or of its governor if the legislature cannot be convened, call into Federal service such of the militia of the other States, in the number requested by that State, and use such of the armed forces, as they consider necessary to suppress the insurrection. Whenever the President considers that unlawful obstructions, combinations, or assemblages, or unjust rebellion against the authority of Pacifica, make it impracticable to enforce the [just] laws of Pacifica in any State by the ordinary course of judicial proceedings, they may call into Federal service such of the militia of any State, and use such of the armed forces, as they consider necessary to enforce those laws or to suppress the rebellion. The President, by using the militia or the armed forces, or both, or by any other means, shall take such measures as they consider necessary to suppress, in a State, any insurrection, domestic violence (generally, not statutory), unlawful combination, or conspiracy, if it: (1) so hinders the execution of the [just] laws of that State, and of Pacifica within the State, that any part or class of its people is deprived of a right, privilege, immunity, or protection named in this Constitution and secured by law, and the constituted authorities of that State are unable, fail, or refuse to protect that right, privilege, or immunity, or to give that protection; or (2) opposes or obstructs the execution of the laws of the Pacifica or impedes the course of justice under those laws. (3) In any situation covered by clause (1), the State shall be considered to have denied the equal protection of the laws secured by this Constitution. They may also call upon the Sheriffs of each County and the Sheriffia in each State to uphold civil order on behalf of Pacifica, insofar as it does not violate any of the [just] laws of their State. Whenever the President considers it necessary to use the militia or the armed forces to repel the dangers to Law and Ordered Liberty as mentioned in this provision, they shall, by proclamation, immediately order the insurgents to disperse and retire peaceably to their abodes within a limited time.

The Presidency is authorized to declare states of national emergency. Such proclamation/s shall immediately be transmitted to the Congress and published in the National Register. Any provisions of law conferring powers and authorities to be exercised during a national emergency shall be effective and remain in effect only when the Presidency has been granted permission to proceed from Congress and such orders are found to be in accordance with the rights of People and resources ensured to them. All declared States of Emergency must be well defined, and clearly specify a criteria why, or date where, such emergency has been declared to end. In the event no such end is in sight, such declaration must be reviewed within each term of two years, and shall be subject to referendum and potential termination by the People [AT ANY TIME] as they shall find needful or [so] desire; Congress is also empowered at any time to end a national emergency, and are required to do so upon majoritarian-consensus in petition by or through direct consultation with their constituents.

In the event that emergency powers are declared, neither the presidency nor any other government official shall seek to circumvent any rights or protections offered under this Constitution.

The presidency may not issue a command, nor shall any act of Congress or the legislature of any State, to confiscate the resources of any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, against parties of Pacifica, its agencies, its officers, or any Person therein.

It is considered un-constitutional for a Presidency to implement executive orders or presidential directives, unless the members of Congress examine, potentially rewrite them, and approve them beforehand with a simple majority. Then they shall be added to the federal statutes.

The Presidency may approve any appropriation or provision and disapprove any other appropriation or provision in the same appropriation bill. In such case they shall, in signing the bill, designate the appropriations and provisions disapproved; and shall return a copy of such appropriations and provisions, with their objections, to the House in which the bill shall have originated; and the same proceedings shall then be had as in case of other bills disapproved by the Presidency.

They shall have Power, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make, alter, or terminate Treaties, provided two-thirds of the Senators present concur; and they shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court, and all other Officers of Pacifica, whose Appointments are not herein otherwise provided for, and which shall be established by Law: but the Congress may by Law vest the Appointment of such inferior Officers, as they think proper, in the Presidency alone, in the Courts of Law, or in the Heads of Departments.

The Presidency shall have Power to fill up all Vacancies that may happen during the Recess of the Senate, by granting Commissions which shall expire at the End of their next Session.

Congress shall define executive privilege. The Presidency, the Vice-President, and any other member of the executive branch may exercise this privilege.

Whenever there is a vacancy in the office of the Vice-President, the Presidency shall nominate a Vice-President who shall take office upon confirmation by a majority vote of both Houses of Congress.

In Case of the Removal of any Consul or of the Presidency from Office, or of their Death, Resignation, or Inability to discharge the Powers and Duties of the said Office, the Same shall devolve on the Vice-President, and the Congress may by Law provide for the Case of Removal, Death, Resignation or Inability, both of the Presidency and Vice-President, declaring what Officers shall then act as Presidency, and such Officers shall act accordingly, until the Disability be removed, or a Presidency shall be elected.

Whenever the Presidency transmits to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives his or her written declaration that he or she are unable to discharge the powers and duties of his or her office, and until he or she transmits to them a written declaration to the contrary, such powers and duties shall be discharged by the Vice-President as Acting President.

Whenever the Vice-President and a majority of either the principal officers of the executive departments or of such other body as Congress may by law provide, transmit to the Presidency pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives their written declaration that the Presidency or any consul/s is/are unable to discharge the powers and duties of their office, the Vice-President shall immediately assume the powers and duties of the office as Acting President Consul. Thereafter, when the President transmits to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives his or her written declaration that no inability exists, he or she shall resume the powers and duties of their office unless the Vice-President and a majority of either the principal officers of the executive department or of such other body as Congress may by law provide, transmit within four days to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives their written declaration that the Presidency or any Consul/s is/are unable to discharge the powers and duties of his or her office. Thereupon Congress shall decide the issue, assembling within forty-eight hours for that purpose if not in session. If the Congress, within twenty-one days after receipt of the latter written declaration, or, if Congress is not in session, within twenty-one days after Congress is required to assemble, determines by two-thirds vote of both Houses that the Presidency or any Consul/s is/are unable to discharge the powers and duties of their office, the Vice-President shall continue to discharge the same as Acting President Consul; otherwise, the Presidency or Consul/s shall resume the powers and duties of their office.

The Presidential Consuls shall be recalled individually from office upon receiving a vote by at least three-fourths of Gubernors of the several States.

SECTION. 3.

They shall from time to time give to the Congress Information of the State of the Union, and recommend to their Consideration such Measures as they shall judge necessary and expedient; they may, on extraordinary Occasions, convene either house, or both of them, and in Case of Disagreement between them, with Respect to the Time of Adjournment, they may adjourn them to such Time as they shall think proper; they shall receive Ambassadors and other public Ministers; they shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed, and shall Commission all the Officers of Pacifica.

If, at the time fixed for the beginning of the term of the Presidency, the President Consul/s elect shall have died, the Vice-President elect shall become President Consul. If a Consul Presidency shall not have been chosen before the time fixed for the beginning of their term, or if the Presidency Consul/s elect shall have failed to qualify, then the Vice-President elect shall act as President Consul until a Presidency of consuls shall have qualified; and the Congress may by law provide for the case wherein neither a Presidency of Consuls elect nor a Vice-President shall have qualified, declaring who shall then act as Presidency, or the manner in which one who is to act shall be selected, and such Person shall act accordingly until a Presidency of Consuls or Vice-President shall have qualified.

SECTION. 4.

The Presidency/Consuls, Vice-President, and all civil Officers of Pacifica, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other Misdemeanors and high Crimes.

ARTICLE V

The legal, law enforcement and investigative functions of the Department of Justice and other legal duties as shall be specified by law shall be vested in one Attorney General, who shall be elected by vote of the people for a term of four years.

The Attorney General shall represent Pacifica and shall conduct the law-enforcement and investigative functions of the department, and all other duties as shall be assigned by law, in conformity with this Constitution, laws made pursuant to it and treaties made or which shall be made under the authority of Pacifica. In conducting their duties, the Attorney General shall at all times safeguard the public interest. The Attorney General is bound to prosecute any case where sufficient evidence exists to charge, regardless of political incentives or motivations to not prosecute.

The Attorney General shall give the President legal advice, in writing, at the President’s request and at other appropriate times and shall inform the President of the actions taken by the Justice Department so far as does not expose the content of an active investigation of the President, and shall attend sessions of the Congress; however, the President may not require the resignation of the Attorney General.

The Attorney General shall from time to time give to the Congress information of the state of the legal and law-enforcement policy and actions of Pacifica, and shall furnish to Congress information requested concerning the same, excepting only such information as may compromise ongoing legal investigations or reveal information properly classified for the purposes of State Security as according to this Constitution.

ARTICLE VI

The Citizens of the several states shall elect by ballot every two years each of the following:

An Administrator of the Department of Finance, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Revenue, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Expenditures, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator as well as a Secretary of the Department of National Treasury, for the National government, and an administrator along with a Secretary for the department of State treasury, for the State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Commerce, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Statistics, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Standards, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Department of Public Works and Internal Improvements, for the National and State governments;

A Director of the Office of Personnel Management, for the national and astate governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Postal Service, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Communications and Public Access Network Commission, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator of the National Patent Office, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Department of Research, Science, Engineering, and Technology, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Open-Source Projects and Information, for the National and State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Public Broadcasting, for the State governments;

An Administrator of the National Archive and Library of Congress, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Department of Public Education, for the State governments;

An Administrator of the Department of Home Relations, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Department of International Relations, for the National government;

An Ambassador as well as a Program Director of the Extraterrestrial/Exobiological Intelligence Recovery and Relations Agency in addition to the EIRRA Recovery Program, and an Administrator over the entire agency, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Department of Defense, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Department of the Navy, for the National government;

A Director of the Agency for Disease Control and Prevention in addition to a head of the ADC’s Prevention’s Pandemic Preparedness unit, for the National government.

An Administrator of the Department of Criminal Jurisprudence and of Pacifican Civil Law, for the National government;

An Administrator of the Department of Reformatory and Criminal Labor, for the National and State governments;

An Attorney General of Pacifica, for the National government;

The Judges of the Supreme Court and such inferior courts of Pacifica and the several States, when there shall be vacancies.

Each of the elected Secretaries and the Chief Attorney shall hold their Offices for a term of two years with a limit of three terms, and the Judges of the Supreme Court and such inferior courts shall serve for a non-renewable term of twelve years.

ARTICLE VII

SECTION. 0.

Natural Justice refers to the rules of fair play, which was originally developed by the courts of equity to control the decisions of inferior courts and then gradually extended to apply equally to the decisions of administrative and domestic tribunals and of any authority exercising an administrative power that affects a person’s status, rights, or liabilities. Any decision reached in contravention of natural justice is void as “ultra vires”.

There are three principal rules in Common Law that are generally referred to in relation to natural justice or procedural fairness. Those are: The Hearing Rule, the Bias Rule, and the Evidence Rule.

The principles of natural justice concern procedural fairness and ensure a fair decision is reached by an objective decision maker. The rules of natural justice provide a minimum standard of procedural fairness and the exact requirements will vary depending on the context.

Maintaining procedural fairness protects the rights of individuals and enhances public confidence in the process.

A word used to refer to situations where audi alteram partem (the right to be heard) and nemo judex in parte sua (no person may judge their own case) apply.

The principles of natural justice were derived from the Romans who believed that some legal principles were “natural” or self-evident and did not require a statutory basis.

These two basic legal safeguards govern all decisions by judges or government officials when they take quasi-judicial or judicial decisions.

Three Common Law rules are referred to in relation to natural justice or procedural fairness.

The Bias Rule:
The first is the rule against bias, i.e. against departure from the standard of even-handed justice required of those who occupy judicial office, ‘nemo judex in causa sua’ (or ‘in propria causa’): no man may be a judge in his own cause. This means that any decision, however fair it may seem, is invalid if made by a person with any financial or other interest in the outcome or any known bias that might have affected his impartiality.
The Bias Rule states that no one should judge his or her own case. This requires the decision maker to be unbiased when holding a hearing or making the decision.
No one ought to be judge in their own case. This is the requirement that the deciding authority must be unbiased when according the hearing or making the decision.
Additionally, investigators and decision-makers must act without bias in all procedures connected with the making of a decision. A decision-maker must be impartial and must make a decision based on a balanced and considered assessment of the information and evidence before him or her without favoring one party over another. Even where no actual bias exists, investigators and decision-makers should be careful to avoid the appearance of bias. Investigators should ensure that there is no conflict of interest which would make it inappropriate for them to conduct the investigation.

The Hearing Rule:
The second rule is known as ‘audi alteram partem’: hear the other side. It states that a decision cannot stand unless the person directly affected by it was given a fair opportunity both to state his case and to know and answer the other side’s case.
The Hearing Rule requires that people must be allowed an opportunity to present their case where their interests and rights may be affected by a decision maker.
To ensure that these rights are respected, the decision maker must give people the opportunity to prepare and present evidence, and to respond to arguments presented by the opposing side.
When conducting an investigation in relation to a complaint, the person being complained against must be advised of the allegations in as much detail as possible and must be given the opportunity to reply to the allegations.

The Evidence Rule:
The third rule is the evidence rule, which connects to Corpus Delicti. It states that an administrative decision must be based upon logical proof or evidence material. Investigators and decision makers should not base their decisions on mere speculation or suspicion. Rather, an investigator or decision maker should be able to clearly point to the evidence on which the inference or determination is based.
Evidence (arguments, allegations, documents, photos, et cetera…) presented by one party must be disclosed to the other party, who may then subject it to scrutiny.

Standing, or locus standi, is the capacity of a party to bring suit in court. If no plaintiff has sustained or will sustain direct injury or harm, then there can be no standing by default. As a general principal, standing to invoke the judicial process requires an actual justiciable controversy as to which the complainant has a real interest in the ultimate adjudication because he or she has either suffered or is about to suffer an injury. Without standing, there is no actual or justiciable controversy, and courts will not entertain such cases.
Typically, the standing inquiry requires careful judicial examination of a complaint’s allegations to ascertain whether the particular plaintiff is entitled to an adjudication of the particular claims asserted. Whether one has standing in a particular case generally revolves around the question whether that person has rights that may suffer some injury, actual or threatened.

SECTION. 0.5.

Pacifican Constitutional Norms of Common Law:

This series of Common Laws inherent to the Pacifican system is not exclusive, and should be developed further by the Courts and Legislatures as is in conformity to their Constitution.

Sub-Section. 0.

The following common law maxims throughout this article shall have the effect and binding force of fixed Judicial Precedent for Military/Maritime, Criminal, Familial, Deportation, and Civil cases, operating both independently and together as is deemed necessary and suitable, so far as the point in which does not produce absurd results or deviate from the zeroth principle of justice, which is Sovereignty of the Individual. The following are some of the more important maxims, but the common law shall not be limited exclusively to these foregoing principles, but rather be expanded to include them, as is appropriate.

Sub-Section. 1.

The common law is created by judicial decisions of process left and to remain un-legislated in the interests of justice alone, and any injustice remedies by then improving upon the common law by statutory law in conjunction to all rights protected by and/or/of [and] through this constitution, and with relevant purpose suitable for equitable case procedure, and is precedent directed by stare decisis.

It is the body of law created by praetors and similar quasi-judicial tribunals by virtue of being stated in written opinions. The defining characteristic of “common law” is that it arises as precedent. In cases where the parties disagree on what the law is, a common law court looks to past precedential decisions of relevant courts, and synthesizes the principles of those past cases as applicable to the current facts. If a similar dispute has been resolved in the past, the court is usually bound to follow the reasoning used in the prior decision (a principle known as stare decisis). If, however, the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases (called a “matter of first impression”), and legislative statutes are either silent or ambiguous on the question, praetors have the authority and duty to resolve the issue (one party or the other has to win, and on disagreements of law, praetors make that decision). The court states an opinion that gives reasons for the decision, and those reasons agglomerate with past decisions as precedent to bind future praetors and litigants. Common law, as the body of law made by praetors, stands in contrast to and on equal footing with statutes which are adopted through the legislative process, and regulations which are promulgated by the executive branch. Stare decisis, the principle that cases should be decided according to consistent principled rules so that similar facts will yield similar results, lies at the heart of all common law systems.

The Congress shall codify the Common Law of Pacifica and fifty-percent-plus-one the several States into Statutes which protect the integrity of the Judicial process from all forms of corruption, as is humanly possible;

Sub-Section. 2.

-Preliminary rules of Common Judicial Process-

In the delivery of writing, not what is said, but what is done is to be considered.

It is to the intention that all law applies.

Precedents has as much law as justice.

The radical element of justice is equality.

Given principles follow their concomitants.

Principles prove, they are not proved.

There is no reasoning of principles.

The principle of a thing is its most powerful part.

There is no disputing against or denying principles.

Abundant caution does no harm.

There should be no departure from common observance or usage, except as perverts the ends of original meaning and intent.

From the words of the law there must be no departure.

What is good and equal, is the law of laws.

Points of law are not laws.

The act of true/natural law does no one an injury.

The [social] contract makes the law.

One who commands lawfully must be obeyed.

Fictions arise from the law, and not law from fictions.

A beneficial law affords a remedy in a similar case.

The law would rather tolerate a private wrong than a public evil.

The law provides for the future, the judge for the past.

Law is the dictate of reason. and a rule of right; The law ought not to fail in dispensing justice. Law is a sacred sanction, commanding what is right and prohibiting the contrary. The law always abhors error and delay.

The law is from everlasting.

Law is the perfection of reason, which commands of its enactors what is useful and necessary and forbids to them the contrary.

The law presumes that one neighbor knows the actions of another.

There must provide proof beyond testimony alone to demonstrate a fact.

The law judges of things which must necessarily be done, as if actually done.

The law of necessity is the law of time, that is, time present.

The law forces no one to do vain or useless things.

The law does wrong to no one. The law never works an injury, or does him a wrong.

The law does nothing and commands nothing in vain.

The law requires nothing impossible.

The law does not regard matters de minimis.

True law forces not to impossibilities.

The law commands not useless things, because useless labor is foolish.

True law does not fail in showing justice.

True law intends not anything impossible.

True law still requires that to be proved, which is otherwise apparent to the court.

The law is the more praised when it is consonant to reason.

The law looks forward, not backward.

True law punishes falsehood.

True law rejects superfluous, contradictory and incongruous things.

The law dislikes delay.

True law always gives a suitable, appropriate, and fair remedy.

True law regards the order of nature.

The laws succor the ignorant.

True law always intends what is agreeable to reason.

The law speaks to all with one mouth.

A common error repeals law; What was at first illegal, being repeated many times, and presumed to have acquired the force of usage, is wrong but to depart from it. Neither does a common error make law; A fault in fact, even if legal by fiat, is still injurious to a person or the integrity of a proceeding.

Error artfully colored is in many things more probable than naked truth; and frequently error conquers truth and reasoning.

Error of law is injurious.

The laws themselves require that they should be governed by right.

The laws of nature are unchangeable. Their enumeration may be subject to [progressive] revisive perfection.

Laws are abrogated or repealed by the same means by which they are made.

An error not resisted is approved.

An error made by a clerk ought not to injure; a clerical error may be corrected.

To refer errors to their origin is to refute them.

An argument from the greater to the less is of no force negatively; conversely it is.

An argument arising from a division is most powerful in law.

An argument drawn from what is inconvenient is good in law, because the law will not permit any inconvenience.

An argument deduced from legitimate authority great avails in law; An argument drawn from legitimate authority is the strongest in law.

An argument drawn from a similar case, or analogy, avails in law.

A twisting of language is unworthy of a judge.

No one is bound to do what is impossible.

Rights are the source and locus of all true law. All rights are not wrongs, and are intrinsic to an Individual's being, as well as to Nature. a law which deviates from protection and promotion and the remainder of necessary safeguards such as but not limited to preservation and defense and service towards the rights of persons and of nature (meaning animals other lifeforms along with the environment).

Sub-Section. 3.

-Relevant to Justice- (Declared)

It is the duty of the government, the law, and justice, to perform fairly.

Power should follow justice, not precede it.

The greatest enemies to peace are force and wrong.

That justice which justly prevents a crime, is better than that which severely punishes it.

No person ought to act against himself; therefore, it is affirmed at all levels, that no person shall be a judge in their own cause; In like manner, no one ought to accuse themself, and all admissions must be corroborated with a Corpus Delicti (Corpus Delicti rule). To conceal is one thing, to be silent another.

Agents and Officers of Law enforcement acting without legal authority are nothing more than common trespassers; A person arrested illegally (or who witnessed such a wrongful arrest) is “provoked” by the threat to liberty and has a right to respond with force. The right to resist an illegitimate arrest provides a complete defense to criminal or civil liability when the person resisted with necessary and sufficient force; Even deadly force can be excused; A person who kills such an agent or officer shall automatically have the legal right to have all charges against them dropped, and in the case of false conviction, pardoned altogether, and in both cases restituted for any of their trouble in such fiasco of public order, if they can show that they were resisting an Un-Lawful and/or Un-Just arrest. An action by an official in excess of their authority is a trespass that may be resisted by physical force; Such trespass against another initiates a provocation which justifies forceful defense, and, if the officer/s is/are killed, is excused, under a person’s Natural Right to resist an unlawful arrest with force to regain and assure liberty. Others may also exercise the common law Citizen’s Police Power, and overtake Military or Law enforcement, and their companions, as well as any impressed person, and demand to see their warrant/s or authorization/s. If the produced response is no warrant or authorization at all, the Citizen’s Police Force may immediately draw their weapons and use them to rescue the impressed Person; If a man be unduly arrested or restrained of their liberty, even if he offers no resistance himself, it remains a provocation to all other Individuals of the Universe, not only friends, or strangers, or even the Country, but also for common humanity sake. Thus, it is no crime to try to rescue the victim of the unlawful arrest because each individual Person is appointed guardian of their fellows’ rights as Pacificans. An Illegal Arrest is an assault and battery; The person attempted to be restrained of their liberty has the same right to use force in defending themself as they would in repelling any other assault and battery; Persons may resist Un-lawful and/or Un-just arrest to the point of taking an arresting officer’s life if necessary; A Person who kills an officer serving an imperfect government warrant cannot be rightly found guilty.

The habitation of each one is an inviolable asylum for him/her/zed. A Person cannot be taken by force from their house to be conducted before a judge or to prison, except according a properly commissioned and issued warrant, in accordance with the rules set forth by the constitution; The maxim in favor of Roman liberty is much the same as that “every Individual’s domicile is their castle.”

A good judge should do nothing from their own judgment, or from the dictates of their private wishes; but he should pronounce according to law and justice.

The judge ought to decide according to the allegation and the proof.

The judge is the speaking law.

A judge cannot be a witness in their own cause.

A judge cannot punish a wrong done to himself.

The judge is condemned when the guilty are acquitted.

The judge does demand more than the plaintiff demands.

To a judge who exceeds their office or jurisdiction no obedience is due.

Judgments frequently become matured by deliberation, never by hurried process.

The latter decisions are stronger in law.

Judgments are, as it were, the dicta or sayings of the law, and are received as truth.

Faith or credit is to be given to the last decisions.

The judge in their decision ought to follow the rule, when the exception is not made apparent.

A judge ought to decide according to the allegations and proofs.

A judgment given by an improper judge is of no moment.

A judgment ought not to be illusory, it ought to have its consequence.

In presumption of law, a judgment is given against inclination.

A judgment is always taken for truth.

The right of blood and kindred cannot be destroyed by any civil law.

The estimation of a crime committed never increases from a subsequent fact.

Sub-Section. 4.

-Relevant to rulings in general- (Declared)

An award is a judgment.

The plaintiff must follow the forum of the thing in dispute.

When the plaintiff does not prove their case, the defendant is absolved.

In criminal cases, the proofs ought to be clearer than the light.

In criminal cases a general intention is sufficient, when there is an act of equal or corresponding degree.

Not every loss produces an injury, yet, no one ought to gain by another’s loss; That which is permitted only at a loss, is not permitted to be done.

The destruction of a thing is a loss received by its owner, except upon consent.

Satisfaction should be made to that fund which has sustained the loss.

Force Majure does no actionable injury; that is, no one is responsible for inevitable accidents.

Sub-Section. 5.

-Pertaining to customary law-

A custom ought to be certain.

Custom is the best expounder of the law.

Custom is another law.

The custom of the place is to be observed.

A prescriptive and legitimate custom overcomes the law.

Custom once disallowed cannot again be produced.

Custom leads the willing, law compels or draws the unwilling.

Whatever by custom is once considered bad, is presumed to be so always, in exactly the same degree.

Reason is the formal cause of custom.

What is done contrary to the custom of our ancestors, neither pleases nor appears right.

Custom is the best interpreter of laws.

A reasonable custom is to be obeyed like law.

An evil custom is meant to be abolished.

A custom introduced against consistent reason ought rather to be called an usurpation than a custom.

Sub-Section. 6.

In doubtful cases the more worthy is to be taken.

In doubtful cases there is no presumption in favor of the will.

In a doubtful case, that is the construction of the law which the words indicate.

In doubt, the gentler course is to be followed.

In doubt, the safer course is to be adopted.

Sub-Section. 7.

-Relevant to Torts- (Declared)

An injurer has no right to remedy, an injury demands remedy.

Sub-Section. 8.

-Of Mistakes/Errs-

It is safer to err on the side of mercy.

The multitude of those who err is no excuse for error.

They who errs does not consent.

Sub-Section. 9.

-Relevant to Fraud- (Declared)

Fraud is odious and not to be presumed.

Fraud lies hidden in general expressions.

Fraud and deceit should excuse no man.

It is a fraud to conceal a fraud.

Fraud and justice never agree together; Thereby, fraud deserving fraud, is a very doubtful morality.

They who acts fraudulently acts in vain.

A deceiver deals in generals.

The fraud of a possessor does not prejudice the successor.

Fraud is not purged by circity.

Out of fraud no lawful action arises.

Right and fraud never go together.

Gross negligence is equal to fraud.

Gross negligence is a fault, gross fault is a fraud.

Great neglect is equivalent to fraud.

Once a fraud, always a fraud.

What is otherwise good and just, if sought by force or fraud, becomes bad and unjust.

It is fraudulent to sell the same thing twice, except upon lawful re-acquisition.

Equity will not allow a statute to be used as a cloak for fraud.

If in a contract for a loan there is inserted a clause that the borrower shall not be answerable for fraud, such clause is void.

Sub-Section. 10.

-Relevant to consent- (Declared)

No one can confirm before the right accrues to him.

A confirmation is null where the preceding gift is invalid.

Consent makes the law. A contract is a law between the parties, which can acquire force only by consent.

Consent removes or obviates a mistake.

Those consenting and those perpetrating are embraced in the same punishment.

No person is bound for the advice they give. Advice, unless fraudulent, does not create an obligation.

Sub-Section. 11.

-Common Law Marriages- (Declared)

The union of a man and a woman is of the law of nature. This does not prohibit civil union, merely observes the obligation of biology to further propagate through reproduction, and all of the synergy between opposite sexes based on their differing strengths and weaknesses, which creates families, close friends, and communities at the core.

The union of husband and wife is founded on the law of nature, not despite it. Building a future through unity and co-creation is a natural beauty, and healthy relationships between healthy spouses in happy houses make healthy families.

Marriages ought to be free.

A subsequent marriage cures preceding criminality.

Neither cohabitation, nor lying together, makes a marriage; it is the consent of the parties which constitutes marriage.

It is not unjust to have two or more wives at one time; Several partners are as one [consular] body [in organizing their actions], by reason of the unity of their rights.

Sub-Section. 12.

-Relevant to customs of government function- (Declared)

The absence of him who is employed in the service of the state, ought not to be burdensome to him nor to any others.

Sub-Section. 13.

-Children and Family Law- (Declared)

Kids born under a legitimate union follow the condition of the father.

They who are in the womb, are considered as born, whenever it is for their benefit.

Not to be born, and to be dead born, is the same.

If a man dies, leaving the mother pregnant, he shall not be considered as having died childless.

Sub-Section. 14.

-Wills, Theyirs, and Inheritances- (Declared)

No one is an heir to the living.

Theyir is a collective name.

Theyir is a term of law, son one of nature.

An heir is either by right of property or right of representation.

An heir is another self, and a son is a part of the father.

The heir is the same person with the ancestor.

The heir of my heir is my heir.

They is the lawful heir whom the marriage demonstrates.

Several co-heirs are as one body, by reason of the unity of right which they possess.

It concerns the commonwealth and the hardiness of our Republic that Person’s last wills be sustained.

Every will is consummated by death.

It concerns the state that the wills of the dead should have their effect.

A holographic will, even without personal statements to the receiver or beneficiar[y]/ies, at the point in which it is discovered, retains equivalence to a final testament.

Inheritance gained by widows must be divided equally among her half, and that other half for her sons, if any, and to the eldest daughter in the case she is without male heirs.

Under this Constitution, there is a common law right to designate one or more ranked “vulgar substitution/s” when holigraphically creating, and officially certifying a will, or in the delivery of testamentary gifts.

-Pertaining to Skies- (Declared)

Sub-Section. 16.

-Pertaining to Waters- (Declared)

Water runs and ought to run.

That which poisons the well, poisons the consumers of that well, and spoils the fruits of all trees which spring from such waters.

Sub-Section. 17.

-Pertaining to Property-

Chattels justly possessed cannot be lost.

Chattels are considered in law among the minor things

Sub-Section. 19.

-Limitations clauses-

No man ought to be wiser than the law [of nature].

They who may condemn may acquit. They who spares the guilty, punishes the innocent.

No one is presumed to be bad. No one is bound to testify to their own baseness. No one is bound to accuse himself. No one alleging their own turpitude is to be heard as a witness.

No one is considered as committing damages, unless he is doing what he has no right to do. They who first offends, causes the strife. No one can truly improve their condition by a crime.

They who offends when drunk or intoxicated, must be punished when sober.

No one can be punished twice for the same crime or misdemeanor.

No one is restrained from using several defenses.

No wise one punishes that things done may be revoked, but that future wrongs may be prevented.

No one is to be punished for the crime or wrong of another.

No one is punished unless for some wrong, act or default.

No one is allowed to incapacitate, or stultify themself, from liability.

No man ought to be burdened in consequence of another’s act.

No one can be a witness in their own cause. But to their rule there are many exceptions.

No man ought to be condemned unheard, unless he be contumacious.

One cannot transfer to another a right which they have not themself

One is not present unless they understand.

No one can verify by the country against a record. The issue upon a record cannot be tried by a jury.

No man can be at the same time tenant and landlord of the same tenement.

No one can do that by another which he cannot do by himself.

No one can owe to himself.

No one should lose their property without their act or negligence. No one can give who does not possess. No one is bound to sell their property, even for a just price.

No one is presumed to give.

No one is bound to arm their adversary.

No man can contradict their own deed. No one is presumed to have preferred another’s posterity to their own.

No one should interfere in what no way concerns him.

No man is presumed to be forgetful of their eternal welfare, and particularly at the point of death.

No one is presumed to trifle at the point of death.

No one is restrained from exercising several kinds of business or arts.

No one is bound to an impossibility.

No one is bound to foretell.

No one is bound to expose himself to misfortune and dangers.

Let him who accuses another be of a clear fame, and not criminal in their own act.

Sub-Section. 20.

-Of life and Death-

Death is denominated the extreme penalty.

To be dead born is not to be born.

The cause ceasing, the effect must cease.

Sub-section. 22.

-On Contracts-

The agreement of the parties makes the law of the contract.

A contract founded on a base and unlawful consideration, or against good morals, is null.

The agreement of the parties overcomes or prevails against the law.

A party that with explicit reservation of rights performs or promises performance or assents to performance in a manner demanded or offered by the other party does not thereby prejudice the right to insist on the full performance of the contract; Nor thereby prejudices the rights reserved. Such words as "without prejudice," "under protest," or the like are sufficient.

Where there is no deed committed, there can be no consequence.

Where there is a right, there is a remedy.

Where the law is uncertain, there is no law.

Where the law compels a man to show cause, the cause ought to be just and legal.

Where the law is special and the reason of it is general, it ought to be taken as being general.

Where the law does not distinguish, we ought not to distinguish.

Where is the greater part, there is the whole.

When the law fails to serve as a rule, almost everything ought to be suspected.

Where there is no authority to enforce, there is no authority to obey.

Where there is no direct law, the opinion of the judges ought to be taken, or reference made to similar cases.

Where there is no law there is no transgression, as it regards the world.

Where there is no principal there is no accessory.

They at whose risk a thing is, should receive the profits arising from it.

Where a thing is concealed generally, ttheir exception arises, that there shall be nothing contrary to law and right.

Let a man be punished when he commits the offence.

Wherever there is a wrong, there damages follow.

The last will of a testator is to be fulfilled according to their true intention.

What is beyond possibility cannot exist, and the reverse, what cannot exist is not possible.

One person can scarcely supply the place of two.

Things universal are better known than things particular.

An university or corporation is not said to do anything unless it be deliberated upon collegiately, although the majority should do it.

One absurdity begin allowed, an infinity follow.

In the same manner in which a thing is bound, it is loosened.

That which is the principal part of a thing is the thing itself.

Everything is dissolved by the same mode in which it is bound together.

Usury is odious in law.

That by the punishment of a few, the fear of it may affect all.

That the thing may rather have effect than be destroyed.

What is useful is not vitiated by the useless.

It shall have effect as far as it can have effect.

Vain is that power which is never brought into action.

Vain are those fears which affect not a valiant man.

Facility of pardon is an incentive to crime.

Words are to be taken so as to have effect.

Equivocal words and those in a doubtful sense are to be taken in their best and most effective sense.

The words current money, refer to the time of payment.

Words spoken of the person are to be understood of the condition of the person.

Words are to be taken most strongly against him who uses them.

General words are to be generally understood.

General words must be confined or restrained to the nature of the subject or the aptitude of the person.

Words ought to be made subservient to the intent, not contrary to it.

Words are to be so understood that the subject-matter may be preserved rather than destroyed.

It is better that words should have no operation, than to operate absurdly.

Words added for the purpose of certainty are to be referred to preceding words, in which certainty is wanting.

Words referred to other words operate chiefly by the reference which appears to be implied towards them.

A verdict is, as it were, the saying of the truth, in the same manner that a judgment is the saying of the law.

The truth of the demonstration removes the error of the name.

Truth fears nothing but concealment.

By too much altercation truth is lost.

They who does not speak the truth, is a traitor to the truth.

A deputy cannot appoint a deputy.

The laws serve the vigilant, not those who sleep upon their rights.

That is a viperous exposition which gnaws or eats out the bowels of the text.

Husband and wife are considered one person in law.

Force is inimical to the laws.

Clerical errors ought not to hurt.

They willed but did not say.

The will of a testator is ambulatory until their death; that is, he may change it at any time.

In offences, the will and not the consequences are to be looked to.

The will is to be taken for the deed.

They who consents cannot receive an injury.

What a man cannot transfer, he cannot bind by articles.

When the Common Law and statute law concur, the Common Law is to be preferred.

When many join in one act, the law says it is the act of him who could best do it; and things should be done by him who has the best skill.

When the law presumes the affirmative, the negative is to be proved.

When no time is limited, the law appoints the most convenient.

When the law gives anything, it gives a remedy for the same.

When the foundation fails, all fails.

Where two rights concur, the more ancient shall be preferred.

–

-Assorted Provisions of Common Law-

They who takes away or destroys the means, destroys the end.

They who decides anything, a party being unheard, though he should decide right, does wrong.

Them who questions and distinguishes well, learns well.

They who grants anything, is considered as granting that, without which their grant would be idle, without which the thing itself could not exist.

They who confirms does not give.

They who contemns the precept, contemns the party giving it.

They who contracts, knows, or ought to know, the quality of the person with whom he contracts, otherwise he is not excusable.

They who ought to inherit from the father, ought to inherit from the son.

They who is born of an illicit union, is not counted among the kids.

They who overthrows the cause, overthrows its future effects.

They who acts by or through another, acts for himself.

They who has jurisdiction to loosen, has jurisdiction to bind.

They who adheres to the letter, adheres to the bark.

They who does not know what he ought to pay, does not want probity in not paying.

They who uses their universal rights, harms no one.

They who does anything by command of a judge, will not be supposed to have acted from an improper motive, because it was necessary to obey.

They who does not willingly speak the truth, is a betrayer of the truth. They who acts badly, hates what is right.

They who proves most, recovers most.

They who betrays their country, is like the insane sailor who bores a hole in the ship which carries him.

They who is born out of lawful matrimony, follows the condition of the mother.

They who fear, take care and avoid. Those are vain fears which do not affect a man of a firm mind.

They who seeks a reason for everything, subverts reason.

They who does not forbid what he can forbid, seems to assent. They who is silent appears to consent. They who does not repel a wrong when he can, induces it. They who does not prevent what he can, seems to commit the thing. They who can and ought to forbid, and does not, commands.

They who does anything through another, is considered as doing it himself.

No one is bound to inform about a thing he knows not, but he who gives information is bound to know what he says. They who says all, excludes nothing.

They who is first or before in time, is stronger in right.

They who obstructs an entrance, destroys a convenience.

They who provides for himself, provides for their heirs.

They who renounces their action once, cannot any more repeat it.

They who is once bad, is presumed to be always so in the same degree, unless proven otherwise.

They who derives a benefit from a thing, ought to feel the disadvantages attending it.

They who pays tardily, pays less than he ought.

Set him who wishes to be deceived, be deceived.

-

It is contrary to the law of nations to violate the rights of ambassadors.

A legacy is confirmed by the death of the testator, in the same manner as a gift from a living person is by delivery alone.

Subsequent laws repeal those before enacted to the contrary.

Laws, not words, are imposed on things.

Human laws are born, live, and die. When laws created by the Human Mind are imposed by ‘the State’ fail, all Persons must act by the Law of Nature, the Rule of Right, and abide by the Precepts of Justice.

Interpretation and reconciliation of the laws so that they harmonize is the best mode of construction.

That construction is to be made so that the subject may have an effect rather than none.

In ambiguous things, such a construction is to be made, that what is inconvenient and absurd is to be avoided.

The construction of just law/s do/es no wrong.

The custom of fixing and refixing (making and annulling) laws is most dangerous.

The construction of law obtains the force of law.

The voice of legislators is a living voice, to impose laws on things and not on words.

The minister of the law is not bound, in the execution of their office, neither to fly nor retreat.

–

Equity acts upon the person.
Equity follows the law.
Natural equity or good faith do not allow us to demand twice the payment of the same thing.
A good judge decides according to justice and right, and prefers equity to strict law.
They who has committed iniquity, shall not have equity.
They who will have equity done to him, must do equity to the same person.
In a fiction of law, equity always subsists.
In all affairs, and principally in those which concern the administration of justice, the rules of equity ought to be followed.
It is against equity for anyone to be judge in their own cause.
It is against equity to deprive freeman of the free disposal of their own property.
A judge ought always to have equity before their eyes.
A judge ought always to regard equity.
Law regards equity.
The law sometimes follows equity.
The law delights in equity; it covets perfection; it is a rule of right.
Law feigns where equity subsists.
Nothing is more conformable to natural equity, than to confirm the will of an owner who desires to transfer their property to another.
Necessity creates equity.
Perpetuities are odious in law and equity.

Reason in law is perfect equity.

Equality is equity.
Equity suffers not a right without a remedy.
Equity looks upon that as done, which ought to be done.
Where there is equal equity, the law must prevail.
